transfer.stem: Which plan preserves visible evidence, the separate exercise and the laboratory instruction?
transfer.passage:
Questions, observations and estimates
Science begins with questions we can investigate. Physics helps explain a boat floating, and a chemistry lesson may include a safe colour-change test. Those records do not supply a chemical recipe or tell anyone to mix unknown materials.
In biology we compared leaf shapes. A separate fictional picture showed one lobed leaf and one smooth oval leaf. It supported comparing outlines, not identifying exact ages or species. Geography helped us understand how rivers shape land, while a museum presented the history of a local railway without giving its opening date.
Maths helped us estimate materials for a shelf. The original sentence did not specify board counts. A separate simplified exercise used two side boards and three shelf boards: five in total. It was a counting exercise, not a complete construction plan. In the laboratory, we wore eye protection. That requirement did not promise that accidents were impossible.

options.text: Compare only visible leaf shapes; treat two plus three boards as a separate exercise; wear eye protection in the laboratory.
Infer exact leaf ages from the picture; treat board counts as a separate exercise; wear eye protection.
Compare visible leaf shapes; claim the original shelf sentence specifies five boards; wear eye protection.
Compare visible leaf shapes; treat board counts as a separate exercise; remove eye protection in the laboratory.

answer.display: Compare only visible leaf shapes; treat two plus three boards as a separate exercise; wear eye protection in the laboratory.
